Executive function across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Intro

This window is characterized not by the emergence of new fundamental executive components, but by the rapid functional integration and tuning of existing capabilities into a coherent system A 2026 multicenter sham-controlled trial reports higher clinical response rates for a digital therapeutic game in children with ADHD (Figure) 50. The trial also reports greater improvement in hyperactivity-impulsivity ratings with the intervention than with sham (Figure).

Executive functions develop particularly rapidly across this window 1

This window marks the transition from childhood to adolescence; adolescence can be seen as a period defined by executive development, or as a period defined by an expansion of the timescales over which goals are pursued 2

This is the developmental window where EF starts to look like reliable online control of a learned world model (state maintenance, state updating, policy selection) in complex real environments like school.

Inhibitory control

Building on the rapid consolidation of basic inhibitory responses observed between ages 7 and 9, ages 9-12 are less about qualitative shifts and more about refining control so it becomes context-sensitive and tightly coupled to goal pursuit, tracking the broader shift from local/concrete to more global/abstract reasoning 3. Empirically, simpler inhibition-heavy tasks often show little additional change across this span (e.g Statue; Knock-and-Tap plateauing after early gains) 4, 5, whereas more complex measures (e.g the Stop-signal task, Eriksen Flankers, and Stroop-like paradigms) demonstrate continued gains in both accuracy and reaction time well into adolescence 6, 7, 8. Functionally, this shows up as more adult-like selective attention (better filtering irrelevant stimuli in noisy or cluttered environments) 9, 10, more reliable delay of gratification, and a steady decline in impulsive responding, so compared to a 9-year-old, a 12-year-old is typically better at staying on-task amid distraction and suppressing locally tempting responses when they conflict with the current rule or longer-horizon outcome, though breakdowns still appear under high affect, fatigue, or complex multi-goal situations that overload coordination across EF subsystems 9, 10, 11, 12. Overall, inhibitory control in 9-12 is in a rapid but advanced phase, characterized by increasing integration with abstract task models and goal hierarchies rather than just raw "stopping power."

Cognitive flexibility

Between the ages of 9 and 12, children make substantial gains in cognitive flexibility, getting much better at representing "what game am I in right now?" and then rapidly reconfiguring itself when the latent task structure changes. Across this window, kids become faster and less error-prone at shifting between rules/dimensions/task sets, increasingly doing so proactively: they use contextual cues to extract goal information ahead of time and prepare the next policy instead of waiting for conflict or errors to force a correction 13, 14. This shows up as steady improvements on intra-/extra-dimensional set shifting 11 and a sharp reduction in switching costs (i.e the performance tax as a result of rule switching) 15, 16. Similar to measurements of inhibitory control, some studies report adult-level switching costs by late in this period 17, 18, 19, while others report advancements well into adolescence 16. In scenarios where rules are mixed, these children see a rapid decrease in mixing costs while remaining far below adult levels 20, 21, 18. In everyday life, these gains show up as smoother transitions between "modes" of behavior: kids more reliably pivot from one classroom routine to another, switch strategies when a problem type changes, follow multi-step instructions that embed conditional rules, and adapt faster when games/sports or social situations introduce a new constraint ("actually, we’re doing it this way now"), all signatures of a world model that’s better at inferring the active latent context and loading the right policy without repeated trial-and-error 13, 14. Remaining limitations are that this flexibility is still more brittle than in adults when cues are ambiguous, stakes/emotion are high, or cognitive load is heavy: children can still perseverate on a prior rule, need external reminders to fully maintain the new task set, and show larger "global" costs in mixed-demand environments where they must keep multiple possible rules online while resisting distraction 16, 14. Overall, ages 9-12 mark a shift toward faster, more proactive context-to-policy switching in the child’s world model, while true adult robustness in messy, high-load real-world settings continues to mature beyond this window. Working memory

Building on the foundational gains of the 7-to-9-year window (where working memory (WM) becomes controllable, interference-resistant, and actively maintained), the 9-12 window is where WM’s functional capacity reliably expands: kids can keep more task-relevant elements simultaneously accessible while running concurrent processing, so WM becomes less about short retention and more about active computation (e.g holding and verifying intermediate results during multi-step computations, maintaining hierarchical rules like "do A unless B, then do C," and tracking multiple constraints while reasoning). Simple span measures continue a largely linear rise across this age range 22, but the more noticeable qualitative jump is on complex span tasks that force genuine time-sharing between storage and processing, which improves sharply and suggests a more efficient division of attentional resources between "maintenance" and "processing" subroutines 23. Performance on spatial working memory tasks also improves rapidly across this window, supporting more reliable mental updating of locations, routes, and object-to-object relations in real time 11. At the same time, this window still shows the classic "easy-task maturity, complex-task immaturity" pattern: some simple maintenance demands plateau early (e.g., holding a face across a delay), while performance continues to develop through adolescence when tasks require strategic exploration, larger search sets, and tighter coordination of memory with planning and control 24. These functional gains are largely supported by metacognitive advancements, as children increasingly deploy maintenance strategies (e.g cumulative rehearsal, semantic grouping, and even external memory stores like notepads) to optimize storage 22. In everyday life, this looks like following multi-step instructions without "losing the thread," doing longer mental computations, and manipulating internal representations more independently of immediate sensory input, capabilities tightly linked to the abstract logical operations that become characteristic of this window 25 and to stronger inductive/deductive reasoning performance 26. Overall, by 12 the child’s mental workspace is noticeably optimized and more stable (able to hold several task-relevant representations online while running computations over them) but it still struggles when tasks demand sustained strategic control (large search spaces, rapid multi-step updating, or tight WM-planning coordination), making performance fragile under high interference, time pressure, or complex goal hierarchies. Planning

Building on the 7-9 shift toward proactive control (where children increasingly pay an up-front compute cost (pre-move deliberation) to reduce downstream errors in branching, multi-step problems) the 9-12 window is where planning starts to look more like a scalable, model-based search routine over an internal world model: children get better at representing deeper action sequences, simulating future states before committing, and choosing subgoals that may temporarily move away from the immediate reward state to enable later success. On classic Tower of London problems, they continue to improve rapidly (especially on the hardest instances), with age-related gains that look like better search control and fewer wasted expansions, and the first-move latency pattern suggests increasing willingness/ability to delay action to allocate more computation to the planning stage 27, 28, 29. On the more naturalistic Zoo Map task (where the child must plan a route through a zoo under multiple constraints), children see similar improvements 30, 31. Prospective memory also strengthens across this span (more reliable "execute the stored intention when the trigger occurs") but remains far from adult-like in consistency, especially under distraction or competing goals 32. Under the hood, episodic future thinking (mentally simulating a specific personal event located in one’s future) becomes richer in detail, has better self-concept coherence, and is increasingly disentangled from current sensory context, though these children still lean more heavily than adults on generalized scripts/semantic scaffolds when simulating 33, 34. In everyday life, these children proactively attend to and anticipate the arrival of important information 25, 2 and begin to appreciate the instrumental value of planning in everyday life 35, 36, a metacognitive insight that supports increasingly future-oriented cognition 37. Overall, 9-12 is where planning becomes a noticeably more model-based, hierarchical "policy synthesis" process, capable of increasingly long-horizon tasks with deeper look-ahead and multi-constraint optimization while still (like the other executive functions) remaining limited by reliability under distraction, cognitive load, and, in general, a lack of knowledge and experience. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Metacognition

Building on the 7-9 window where metacognitive monitoring becomes behaviorally actionable (children can represent "I don’t know," use confidence/uncertainty to regulate responding, and begin catching inconsistencies in their own reasoning), the 9-12 window is where metacognition starts to operate more like a meta-level controller that (i) selects strategies, (ii) rationally allocates compute/effort and (iii) maintains better-calibrated uncertainty over an expanding hypothesis space. Longitudinal work shows that shifts from nonstrategic to strategic behavior can arrive suddenly during this window: once children discover an effective organizational policy (e.g sorting/grouping to support recall), performance can jump immediately, consistent with a discrete "strategy induction" event rather than slow parameter tuning 38. Concurrently, memory monitoring and uncertainty estimation improve rapidly under cued recall, and kids become more reliable at reading out subjective cues (e.g fluency, latency, effort) to infer whether they actually know something, though systematic overconfidence still remains common 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44. At the level of control, children become much more sensitive to the cost of cognitive effort, rationally allocating resources according to task demands and potential rewards in a way that is far more explicit than at nine 45 (a signature of arbitration between competing internal systems 46), though this capacity likely remains domain-/context-specific across this window 47. In terms of their fundamental epistemological stances, these children begin to disentangle the nature of the unknown: they increasingly distinguish between epistemic uncertainty (missing information that can be learned) and aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible noise), alongside a shift from "absolutist" (knowledge consists of certain facts about the world; binary truth) to "multiplist/relativist" (knowledge is inherently subjective and uncertain) views of knowledge.

In everyday life, these upgrades show up as children increasingly "closing the loop" between monitoring and control: they check for narrative coherence and completeness while reading, explaining, or writing ("does that make sense?", "did I include the key causal links?", "what evidence supports this claim?"), and they revise more deliberately when they detect gaps or contradictions, rather than only polishing surface features. The same meta-level controller increasingly supports active learning: kids more often treat learning actions (asking a question, looking something up, re-reading, practicing one more problem) as choices with explicit costs, and they become better at trading off effort/time against expected information gain, gathering more evidence when it is cheap and stopping earlier when information acquisition is costly or low-yield. Finally, instead of collapsing prematurely onto a single story about "what’s going on," they more often maintain a small superposition of plausible hypotheses (especially in ambiguous social/causal situations), using uncertainty to delay commitment until enough discriminative evidence accumulates. Overall, metacognition from 9-12 increasingly behaves like a rational meta-controller, improving strategy discovery, calibration, and evidence-seeking, yet internal signals remain noisy (i.e still overconfident) and emotionally entangled (i.e perceived difficulty can still trigger persistent coping policies like frustration, blame shifting, disengagement, or magical thinking) 48, and their epistemology typically has not stabilized into a fully "evaluativist" stance where disagreements are adjudicated by systematically weighting evidence and argument coherence rather than being treated as mere perspective (e.g when two kids tell different stories about what happened, they’ll treat it as "he said/she said" rather than asking what each person actually observed and how reliable that observation was). Summary and conclusion

Conclusion

by about age ?, most children maintain an implicit, globally consistent 3D scene representation with object individuation, coarse material/affordance labels, and simple physical dynamics sufficient for planning and re-planning, while adultlike metric precision, cue-combination, and multi-object dynamics mature from ?-?. What is the state of the cognitive map (across resolutions)?

Transitioning into adolescence

They understand logical principles when applied to familiar, tangible situations but have difficulty applying the same principles to abstract concepts or imaginary scenarios.

These children are "zooming out" and beginning to focus on abstracting from their immediate environments; one way this shows up is in the more-rapid advancement of extrinsic (between-object relationships) spatial cognition relative to intrinsic (within-object relationships) 49
